prompt: How does the hydroxyl group of a phenol affect electrophilic aromatic substitution?

choices.text: It is a strongly activating, ortho- and para-directing substituent
It is a strongly deactivating, meta-directing substituent
choices.why: The –OH group activates the ring; phenols are highly reactive substrates.

choices.text: It is a weakly deactivating, ortho- and para-directing substituent
choices.why: That pattern belongs to the halogens (Section 16.4). The –OH group is strongly activating.

choices.text: It is a strongly activating, meta-directing substituent
choices.why: The –OH group directs incoming groups to the ortho and para positions.

explanation: The hydroxyl group is a strongly activating, ortho- and para-directing substituent. As a result, phenols are highly reactive substrates for electrophilic halogenation, nitration, sulfonation, and Friedel–Crafts reactions.

prompt: Phenol undergoes electrophilic nitration. Where on the ring does the nitro group go?

choices.text: Ortho and para to the –OH group
Meta to the –OH group
choices.why: The –OH group is an ortho- and para-director.

choices.text: Ortho only, because para is too far from the –OH
choices.why: Both the ortho and para positions are activated by the –OH group.

choices.text: Nowhere, because the –OH group deactivates the ring
choices.why: The –OH group strongly activates the ring, making phenols highly reactive toward nitration.

explanation: Because the –OH group is strongly activating and ortho- and para-directing, an electrophile such as the nitronium ion substitutes at the ortho and para positions, giving o- and p-nitrophenol.

prompt: Why don't phenols undergo oxidation the same way alcohols do?

choices.text: They have no hydrogen atom on the hydroxyl-bearing carbon
They have no hydrogen on the oxygen
choices.why: Phenols do have an O–H hydrogen; it's what makes them acidic.

choices.text: Their ring is too electron-poor to be oxidized
choices.why: The –OH group makes a phenol ring electron-rich and strongly activated.

choices.text: Aromatic compounds can't be oxidized at all
choices.why: Phenols are oxidized; the products are quinones.

explanation: Phenols don't undergo oxidation in the same way as alcohols because they don't have a hydrogen atom on the hydroxyl-bearing carbon. Instead, oxidation of a phenol yields a quinone.

prompt: What kind of product forms when a phenol is oxidized?

choices.text: A quinone, a 2,5-cyclohexadiene-1,4-dione
A hydroquinone, a p-dihydroxybenzene
choices.why: Hydroquinones are the reduced partners of quinones; quinones are reduced to hydroquinones.

choices.text: Cyclohexanone
choices.why: The product keeps two C=C bonds in the ring and has two C=O groups.

choices.text: Benzoic acid
choices.why: No carbon is added; the two carbonyl groups form on ring carbons 1 and 4.

explanation: Oxidation of a phenol yields a 2,5-cyclohexadiene-1,4-dione, or quinone. Phenol itself is oxidized by sodium dichromate to benzoquinone in 79% yield.

prompt: What is Fremy's salt, which is often used to oxidize phenols to quinones?

choices.text: Potassium nitrosodisulfonate, (KSO3)2NO
Sodium dichromate, Na2Cr2O7
choices.why: Sodium dichromate also oxidizes phenol to benzoquinone, but it isn't Fremy's salt.

choices.text: Tin(II) chloride, SnCl2
choices.why: SnCl2 is a reducing agent; it converts quinones to hydroquinones.

choices.text: Sodium borohydride, NaBH4
choices.why: NaBH4 is a reducing agent; it converts quinones to hydroquinones.

explanation: Many oxidizing agents convert phenols to quinones, but potassium nitrosodisulfonate, (KSO3)2NO, called Fremy's salt, is often used.

prompt: What forms when a quinone is reduced with NaBH4 or SnCl2?

choices.text: A hydroquinone, a p-dihydroxybenzene
Phenol
choices.why: Reduction turns both C=O groups into –OH groups, so the product has two –OH groups, not one.

choices.text: Cyclohexane-1,4-diol
choices.why: The ring becomes aromatic again; only the two C=O groups are converted into –OH groups.

choices.text: Nothing, because quinones can't be reduced
choices.why: Quinones are easily reduced. Their redox properties are what make them valuable.

explanation: Quinones are valuable because of their redox properties. They are easily reduced to hydroquinones (p-dihydroxybenzenes) by reagents such as NaBH4 and SnCl2, and hydroquinones are easily reoxidized back to quinones.

prompt: Which statement about ubiquinones (coenzymes Q) is correct?

choices.text: They occur in the cells of all aerobic organisms, from bacteria to humans
They occur only in green plants and a few kinds of bacteria
choices.why: Ubiquinones are found in all aerobic organisms, which is why they are named for their ubiquitous occurrence.

choices.text: They are used up in each turn of the respiration cycle
choices.why: Ubiquinone acts only as an intermediary and is itself unchanged.

choices.text: They function in the cell nucleus rather than in the mitochondria
choices.why: Ubiquinones function within the mitochondria of cells.

explanation: Ubiquinones, also called coenzymes Q, are components of the cells of all aerobic organisms, from the simplest bacterium to humans, and are named for their ubiquitous occurrence. They act as biochemical oxidizing agents in the mitochondria, mediating the electron transfer involved in energy production.

prompt: In the respiration process that ubiquinones mediate, what is the overall result?

choices.text: NADH is oxidized to NAD+, O2 is reduced to water, and energy is produced
NAD+ is reduced to NADH, and water is oxidized to O2
choices.why: That is the reverse direction. Electrons are carried from NADH to O2.

choices.text: Ubiquinone is converted into hydroquinone as the final product
choices.why: Ubiquinone acts only as an intermediary and is unchanged overall.

choices.text: NADH is oxidized to NAD+, and O2 is reduced to H2O2
choices.why: O2 ends up as water.

explanation: Ubiquinones function within the mitochondria to mediate respiration, in which electrons are transported from the biological reducing agent NADH to molecular oxygen. NADH is oxidized to NAD+, O2 is reduced to water, and energy is produced; ubiquinone is unchanged.

prompt: Phenol is oxidized by sodium dichromate to benzoquinone in 79% yield. How many moles of benzoquinone would 0.400 mol of phenol give?
How many C=O groups does a quinone, 2,5-cyclohexadiene-1,4-dione, contain?
explanation: The suffix -dione means two ketone C=O groups, here on ring carbons 1 and 4. The ring also keeps two C=C bonds, at carbons 2 and 5 (2,5-cyclohexadiene).
